category.title: Advanced Trees & Self-Balancing Trees
category.description: Self-balancing binary search trees, multi-way indexing trees, randomized trees, and amortized data structures including AVL, Red-Black, B-Tree, B+ Tree, Treap, and Splay Tree.

algorithms.title: AVL Tree (LL, RR, LR, RL Rotations)
algorithms.summary: Height-balanced Binary Search Tree where balance factor |height(left) - height(right)| <= 1 is maintained via LL, RR, LR, and RL rotations.
explanation: 1. Balance Factor: `BF(node) = height(node.left) - height(node.right)`.
2. Left-Left (LL) Case: Unbalance in left child's left subtree -> Perform Right Rotation.
3. Right-Right (RR) Case: Unbalance in right child's right subtree -> Perform Left Rotation.
4. Left-Right (LR) Case: Unbalance in left child's right subtree -> Perform Left Rotation on left child, then Right Rotation on node.
5. Right-Left (RL) Case: Unbalance in right child's left subtree -> Perform Right Rotation on right child, then Left Rotation on node.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Insert 10, 20, 30 into empty AVL Tree
traceSteps: Insert 10: Root 10, Height=1, BF=0.
Insert 20: 10 -> right: 20. Height(10)=2, BF=-1.
Insert 30: 20 -> right: 30. Height(10)=3, Height(20)=2, BF(10) = -2 (Unbalanced RR Case!).
Perform Left Rotation on 10: 20 becomes new root, left child 10, right child 30.
Result: Height-balanced tree with Root=20, Left=10, Right=30.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Guarantees strict O(log N) worst-case search time by keeping tree strictly height balanced.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When read-heavy search queries dominate and strict upper bound on tree height is needed.
wAnswers.whereUsed: In-memory database index structures, real-time lookup dictionaries.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Strict balance limit guarantees height <= 1.44 * log2(N).

algorithms.title: Red-Black Tree (Recoloring & Tree Rotations)
algorithms.summary: Self-balancing binary search tree where each node is colored RED or BLACK, maintaining balance through color rules and rotations.
explanation: 1. Red-Black Invariants: Root is always BLACK. Every leaf (NIL) is BLACK. No two consecutive RED nodes (Red Property). Every path from node to descendant leaves contains same number of BLACK nodes (Black Height).
2. Insert Logic: Insert new node as RED. If parent is RED, violation occurs (Double Red).
3. Case 1 (Uncle is RED): Recolor parent and uncle to BLACK, grandparent to RED.
4. Case 2 (Uncle is BLACK, Triangle): Rotate parent to transform into Case 3 line configuration.
5. Case 3 (Uncle is BLACK, Line): Rotate grandparent and swap colors of parent and grandparent.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Insert elements into Red-Black Tree
traceSteps: Insert 10: Root colored BLACK.
Insert 20: Right child colored RED. (No violation).
Insert 30: Double RED violation (20-RED, 30-RED). Uncle is NIL-BLACK.
Perform Left Rotation at 10 and swap colors of 10 and 20.
Result: 20-BLACK root, 10-RED left, 30-RED right. All Red-Black properties satisfied!

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Maintains balanced search tree with fewer rotations during insertion/deletion compared to AVL trees.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When frequent insertions and deletions occur in ordered maps and sets.
wAnswers.whereUsed: C++ STL `std::map` / `std::set`, Java `TreeMap` / `TreeSet`, Linux kernel CFS scheduler.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Guarantees max 2 rotations per insertion and at most 3 rotations per deletion.

algorithms.title: B-Tree (Multi-Way Search Tree for Databases)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log_M N) Disk Reads, Search, Insert
algorithms.summary: Self-balancing M-way search tree optimized for systems reading/writing large blocks of disk memory (Databases & File Systems).
explanation: 1. Order M: Every node can contain at most `M-1` keys and `M` children.
2. All leaf nodes are at the same depth level.
3. Node Splitting: When a node overflows (`M` keys), the median key is pushed up to the parent node and the node splits into two halves.
4. High Fanout: Large `M` (e.g. M=1024) minimizes disk I/O seek operations by storing hundreds of keys per block node.

exampleTrace.title: Trace B-Tree Order 3 (Max 2 keys per node)
traceSteps: Insert keys 10, 20 into root: Node = [10, 20].
Insert 30: Node overflows [10, 20, 30]! Median 20 moves up as new Root.
Left child = [10], Right child = [30].
Height stays perfectly balanced at 2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Reduces disk I/O latency when managing vast databases stored on block storage.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When data resides on disk and block read operations are expensive.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Relational databases (PostgreSQL, SQLite), ext4 / NTFS file systems.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(log_M N) height requires minimal disk head movements.

algorithms.title: B+ Tree (Leaf-Linked Indexing)
algorithms.summary: Variation of B-Tree where data records reside exclusively in leaf nodes and leaves are connected in a linked list for ultra-fast range queries.
explanation: 1. Internal nodes store ONLY routing keys (no actual data pointers), enabling much larger fanout per node block.
2. Leaf Level: Every data record resides in a leaf node.
3. Doubly Linked Leaf List: All leaf nodes are linked sequentially (`leaf.next`), allowing full range scans `WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 100` without re-traversing internal tree nodes.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Range Scan [15 to 45] on B+ Tree
traceSteps: Traverse down internal nodes to locate starting leaf for key 15 in O(log_M N).
Read records at leaf node.
Follow pointer `leaf.next` sequentially to traverse contiguous leaf blocks.
Stop range scan once key > 45. (Zero tree re-traversals!).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Optimizes sequential range scans in relational databases while maintaining logarithmic point lookups.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When database workload requires both point queries (`WHERE id = x`) and range scans (`WHERE id BETWEEN a AND b`).
wAnswers.whereUsed: MySQL InnoDB storage engine, Oracle DB, NTFS file system indexes.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Linked leaf layer turns range queries into sequential linear scans.

algorithms.title: Treap (Randomized BST with Split & Merge)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log N) Expected Search, Split, Merge
algorithms.summary: Randomized data structure combining Binary Search Tree property on keys with Heap property on randomly generated priorities.
explanation: 1. Dual Invariant: BST ordering on key `val` and Max-Heap ordering on random priority `priority`.
2. Split Operation: `split(root, key)` splits tree into two Treaps `T1` (keys <= key) and `T2` (keys > key) in O(log N).
3. Merge Operation: `merge(T1, T2)` combines two Treaps into one (assuming max_key(T1) < min_key(T2)) in O(log N).
4. High probabilistic balance: Random priority assignment ensures expected height remains logarithmic O(log N) without complex explicit balancing rules.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Split Treap at key K=15
traceSteps: Treap contains keys [5, 10, 15, 20, 25] with max-heap priority nodes.
Execute Split at K=15.
Left Treap T1 contains [5, 10, 15] maintaining priority heap order.
Right Treap T2 contains [20, 25] maintaining priority heap order.
Operation completes recursively in O(log N) steps.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides extremely clean implementation of balanced BSTs with non-trivial range cut/paste operations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When building implicit treaps for dynamic array operations (rope data structures, interval moves).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Rope data structure text editors, randomized order-statistic trees.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Split and Merge primitives make complex tree restructuring effortless.

algorithms.title: Splay Tree (Splaying & Amortized O(log N))
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log N) Amortized time per operation
algorithms.summary: Self-adjusting binary search tree that moves recently accessed nodes to the root using Splaying rotations (Zig, Zag, Zig-Zig, Zag-Zag).
explanation: 1. Locality Principle: Frequently accessed elements stay near the root for ultra-fast repeated access.
2. Splay Operation: Whenever a node is searched, inserted, or updated, it is splayed to the root via tree rotations.
3. Zig Step: Single rotation when target's parent is root.
4. Zig-Zig / Zag-Zag Step: Double rotation in same direction when node and parent are both left or both right children.
5. Zig-Zag / Zag-Zig Step: Double rotation in opposite directions when node and parent are opposite children.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Splay key 10 to Root
traceSteps: Access node 10 at depth 3.
Check parent & grandparent configuration.
Apply Zig-Zig or Zig-Zag double rotations.
Node 10 ascends directly to become new Root.
Tree balance improves along access path.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Achieves O(log N) amortized performance without storing balance factor or color bits at nodes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When data accesses exhibit temporal locality (recently accessed items accessed again).
wAnswers.whereUsed: GC garbage collection memory allocators, network packet cache routers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Zero explicit balance metadata per node, automatically self-optimizes based on access patterns.
